papers.title: Prime Accessible Deterministic Automata
papers.abstract: We classify prime accessible deterministic automata over finite alphabets, both among finite automata and among automata with arbitrary state sets. Every one-state automaton is prime. Over a one-letter alphabet, a finite nontrivial automaton is prime exactly when it is a cycle of prime-power length or a finite chain ending in a fixed state. The unique infinite accessible unary automaton, up to isomorphism, is also prime. Every nontrivial automaton over an alphabet with at least two letters is not prime. Shen proved the finite case; we give a shorter proof. We also characterize a decomposition of the automaton whose states are all finite input words. The reachable product of the quotients by the least right congruences identifying the empty word with nonempty words $p$ and $q$, respectively, is isomorphic to this automaton exactly when $p^r\ne q^s$ for all positive integers $r,s$.

papers.title: Limit-sure Winning in Team Games without Shared Randomness
papers.abstract: We study concurrent stochastic games in which a team of agents plays against an adversarial environment. If the agents could access a shared source of randomness, then these games reduce to two-player games. Despite being common in the literature on coalition games, this assumption does not accurately model real-world systems. In this paper, we consider the setting where the agents only have access to individual sources of randomness, and must satisfy a given reachability or safety objective. The limit-sure problem asks whether the team can ensure that the objective is satisfied with probability at least $1-\lambda$ for every $\lambda>0$. For reachability objectives, we show that this problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete. For safety objectives, we show that limit-sure winning coincides with almost-sure winning, which is known to lie in $\mathsf{P}$. As a corollary of these results, we conclude that model checking of the qualitative fragment of the logic Individually Randomised ATL -- introduced in the recent work of Brice et al. -- is $\mathsf{P}^{\mathsf{NP}}$-complete.

papers.title: The Smallest String Attractors of Fibonacci, Period-Doubling, and Thue--Morse Words
papers.abstract: A string attractor of a string $T[1..|T|]$ is a set of positions $\Gamma$ of $T$ such that any nonempty substring $w$ of $T$ has an occurrence that crosses a position in $\Gamma$, i.e., there is a position $i$ such that $w = T[i..i+|w|-1]$ and the intersection $[i,i+|w|-1]\cap \Gamma$ is nonempty. The size of the smallest string attractor of Fibonacci words and period-doubling words of length at least $2$ is known to be $2$. The size of the smallest string attractor of Thue--Morse words of length at least $25$ is known to be $4$. We completely characterize the set of all smallest string attractors of Fibonacci words, period-doubling words, and Thue--Morse words. For Fibonacci words, we show a recursive formula describing the $2^{n-4} + 2^{\lceil n/2 \rceil - 2}$ distinct position pairs that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th Fibonacci word for $n \geq 7$. For period-doubling words, we show a formula describing the two distinct position pairs that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th period-doubling word for $n\geq 2$. For Thue--Morse words, we show a formula describing the 32 sets of four positions that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th Thue--Morse word for $n\geq 6$. Our results show that strings with the same smallest attractor size can have a drastically different number of distinct smallest attractors.

papers.title: A Unifying Framework for Global Optimization: From Theory to Formalization
papers.abstract: We introduce an abstract measure___theoretic framework that serves as a tool to rigorously study stochastic iterative global optimization algorithms as a unified class. The framework is formulated in terms of probability kernels, which, via the Ionescu--Tulcea theorem, induce probability measures on the space of sequences of algorithm iterations, endowed with two intuitive properties. This framework answers the need for a general, implementation___independent formalism in the analysis of such algorithms, providing a starting point for formalizing global optimization results in proof-assistants. To illustrate the relevance of our tool, we show that common algorithms fit naturally in the framework, and we also use it to give a rigorous proof of a general consistency theorem for stochastic iterative global optimization algorithms (Proposition 3 of (Malherbe, et al., 2017). This proof and the entire framework are formalized in the Lean proof assistant. This formalization both ensures the correctness of the definitions and proofs, and provides a basis for future machine-assisted formalizations in the field.

papers.title: Checking and producing word attractors
papers.abstract: The article focuses on word (or string) attractors, which are sets of positions related to the text compression efficiency of the underlying word. The article presents two combinatorial algorithms based on Suffix automata or Directed Acyclic Word Graphs. The first algorithm decides in linear time whether a set of positions on the word is an attractor of the word. The second algorithm generates an attractor for a given word in a greedy manner. Although the problem of generating a smallest attractor is NP-hard, {the algorithm is efficient and produces very small attractors and even the smallest ones for several well-known infinite families of words.

papers.title: Quantitative Verification of Infinite-State Networks
papers.abstract: Many network protocols and distributed systems combine recursion, unbounded local state, and quantitative behaviour such as cost, latency, or reliability. Existing decidability results for networks of pushdown systems are largely qualitative, and do not extend to quantitative analyses, which must jointly track traces and weights. We present a framework for the quantitative verification of acyclic networks of weighted pushdown systems. Finitely summarising a recursive network component requires collapsing the infinite family of runs obtained by pumping its nested loops, and doing so exactly, rather than by over-approximation, is a standing difficulty. We give a class of weight domains where this is possible: pumping semirings, those in which the weights accumulated by such a family collapse to a closed form; informally, the domain must be unable to count iterations. The class admits domains with infinite ascending chains, such as the arctic semiring and downward-closed languages. Over these, we give a terminating saturation algorithm computing quantitative reachability exactly, resting on two ideas: segment tree algebras, a compositional representation of runs, and thermal extensions, which symbolically separate accelerated weights so that further acceleration remains exact. We use this to compute upward and downward closures of context-free languages uniformly, and to lift the algorithm to acyclic networks over "thin" pumping semirings, yielding the first quantitative safety and reachability analyses for networks of pushdown systems.
